analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans import lower-priced prescription drugs from Canada and other approved countries with safety safeguards.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill with 33 Senate cosponsors to let Americans import cheaper prescription drugs got one hearing and was never voted on, dying in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let Americans legally buy prescription drugs from Canada and other countries with U.S.-equivalent safety systems, either in person by mail for personal use or in bulk through registered pharmacies and wholesalers. It included a detailed safety framework — registered exporters and importers, FDA inspections, verified supply chains, and bans on drug companies punishing or cutting off anyone who imports. The bill never got a vote in the Senate committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who buy prescription drugs — especially seniors on fixed incomes — would gain access to the same FDA-approved medicines sold at lower prices in Canada and other wealthy countries. The bill's own findings state Americans pay up to five times more than consumers elsewhere and estimate savings of at least $38 billion a year. People could import up to a 90-day personal supply directly, and pharmacies and wholesalers could import in bulk, increasing competition.

how_it_helps.text: Would waive the current ban on importing U.S.-made prescription drugs back into the United States, allowing individuals to order up to a 90-day personal supply from registered exporters in Canada and other approved countries (Australia, EU members, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland)
Would let registered pharmacies, groups of pharmacies, and wholesalers import qualifying drugs in bulk, using competition from lower foreign prices to push down what Americans pay

Would make it unlawful for manufacturers to discriminate against importers with higher prices, cut off or delay their supplies, refuse to do business with them, or engineer differences between the U.S. version of a drug and the version sold abroad — enforced by the FTC and state attorneys general with triple damages
Would declare that reselling in the U.S. a drug properly sold abroad is not patent infringement, closing a legal avenue companies could use to block imports

Would build a safety system rather than a free-for-all: importers and exporters must register with the FDA, submit to inspections at least 12 times a year, verify the chain of custody from the manufacturer, post bonds, mark compliant shipments with anticounterfeiting technology, and sell only FDA-approved drugs with U.S. labeling; controlled substances, biologics, and injected or infused drugs are excluded

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost: they would lose the ability to keep cheaper identical drugs sold abroad out of the U.S. market, would be barred from charging different prices to punish exporters, and would have to notify the FDA of any differences between U.S. and foreign versions of their drugs. Importers and exporters would pay registration and inspection fees to fund the oversight system.

drawbacks.text: Opponents argued imported drugs could be counterfeit, substandard, or mishandled; the bill answers this with registration, FDA inspections, chain-of-custody verification, and anticounterfeiting marks, but no inspection regime can catch every bad shipment, and the FDA would need to build substantial new capacity

The $38 billion-a-year savings figure is the bill's own congressional finding, not an independent estimate; actual savings depend on how much supply drug makers make available abroad, and companies responded to earlier importation laws by limiting Canadian exports

The bill relies on manufacturers voluntarily selling drugs in permitted countries; it cannot compel a company to sell a drug in Canada or Europe at all, so a company willing to withdraw from those markets could defeat importation for its products
Heavier foreign demand driven by U.S. importation could tighten drug supplies and raise prices in the exporting countries, including Canada

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit for Americans who buy prescription drugs is large — access to the same FDA-approved medicines at the prices paid in other wealthy countries, with the bill's own findings claiming tens of billions in annual savings. The costs are real but manageable: the oversight system is funded by fees on importers and exporters rather than taxpayers, and the main unresolved risks are enforcement capacity at the FDA and the chance that manufacturers simply restrict foreign supply, which would shrink the savings. The safety design is unusually detailed for an importation bill, which makes the decision to let it die without a vote harder to defend on safety grounds alone.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate health committee for nearly two years, got one hearing, and was never brought up for a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 9, 2005, with a bipartisan list of 33 cosponsors — 25 Democrats, 7 Republicans, and 1 Independent — including Grassley, McCain, Snowe, Lott, and Collins
It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on February 9, 2005
The committee held hearings on the bill on April 19, 2005, printed as S.Hrg. 109-143
After the hearings, no further action was ever taken — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007
The bill's stated premise was that Americans pay up to five times more for the same drugs than consumers abroad and that open pharmaceutical markets could save consumers at least $38 billion a year

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off because the bill died: the two-tier pricing system that lets them charge Americans far more than consumers in other countries stayed intact. Canadians and other foreign consumers also avoided the supply pressure that large-scale U.S. importation would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept higher U.S. prices

for.name: Sen. Byron Dorgan (D-ND)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave repeated floor statements explaining that Americans pay up to five times more for the same drugs sold abroad

for.name: Cosponsoring senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Republicans Snowe, Grassley, McCain, Chafee, Lott, and Collins, giving it support from both parties

for.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and brand-name drug companies
for.what_they_did: Ran a campaign against legalizing prescription drug importation, warning of safety risks and lobbying to keep the ban in place

against.name: Sen. Mike Enzi (R-WY)
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee where the bill sat; held one round of hearings in April 2005 but never scheduled a vote or a markup, and the bill died there when the 109th Congress ended

against.name: President George W. Bush and his health officials
against.what_they_did: Opposed legalizing drug importation on safety grounds and sided with the industry position during this period

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — the bill was introduced with prominent Democrats and Republicans and gathered 25 Democratic, 7 Republican, and 1 Independent cosponsor — but the Republican-run committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would end the industry's ability to charge Americans far more for the same drugs sold in Canada, Europe, Japan, and elsewhere, and would outlaw supply cutoffs, refusals to deal, and formulation changes aimed at blocking importation — with FTC and state attorney general enforcement and triple damages.

industries.industry: Canadian and foreign internet and retail pharmacies
industries.note: Canadian pharmacies and exporters in other permitted countries could register to sell directly to American consumers and U.S. wholesalers, creating a new legal market that the current import ban largely blocks.
Pharmacies and wholesalers could register as importers and buy cheaper drugs abroad, but they would also face new price competition from direct-to-consumer importation by individuals.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: The bill explicitly leaves untouched the rebates and formulary payments manufacturers make to pharmacy benefit managers and insurers, preserving the intermediary structure through which much of U.S. drug pricing flows.
